newsitem.title: UK: Syria says Clinton must push for Middle East peace.
newsitem.headline: Syria says Clinton must push for Middle East peace.

text.p: Syria said on Tuesday that U.S. President Bill Clinton was morally obliged to give a boost to the ailing Middle East peace process and Washington did not have the right to walk away from the problem.
Syrian Foreign Affairs Minister Farouq al-Shara said the United States, as one of the co-sponsors of the peace process, had to finish what it had helped to start.
"It is not for President Clinton, now that he has been re-elected, to say: "Now I am more interested in the eastern hemisphere, or Asia, or Russia'," al-Shara said.

"It will have something to do with the credibility of the United States at the highest level if it doesn't revive the efforts, in a forceful way, to achieve the objectives which it set out," he told a news conference.
Al-Shara also called on the European Union to make more of a contribution, saying it was evident Washington needed help.
"It would be a waste of time if we threw all of what we had achieved into the sea," said the minister, in London for talks with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
"I don't think the people and the international community would like to see the peace process starting from scratch. This will ignite all the old hatreds and mistrust."

U.S. foreign policy analysts say impending changes at the State Department after Clinton's November victory are adding to the sense of drift in the Middle East, as ties between Israel, the Palestinians and Syria become increasingly frayed.
"Five years ago the United States saw itself as a supersonic state. People told themselves: "If we want something, we can get it.' But (Middle East peace) has not yet been achieved," al-Shara said.
"That's why the United States needs some other partners, not to compete with or replace it, but to help. European help is a must," he said.
Israel and Syria have held sporadic peace talks for five years but never managed to solve the problem of the Golan Heights, which Israeli troops occupied during the 1967 Middle East War.
Israel's previous government, ousted by hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May elections, said it could make a partial withdrawal for full peace.
Syria claimed Israel had in fact agreed to a full withdrawal and said the United States held all the relevant documents.
But Washington has signalled it sees no point in trying to persuade the two sides to talk and U.S. officials now believe Syria was never ready to strike a deal with Israel.
Netanyahu's government has further infuriated Arabs by pushing ahead with plans to expand Jewish settlements in the West Bank and on the Golan Heights.
